title: API design
description: Resources, methods, and status codes; pagination and versioning; safe retries; and picking the right protocol.

lessons.title: Resources and methods
lessons.summary: Nouns in the path, verbs in the method, and status codes that say what happened.

steps.prompt: Which request best follows REST conventions for deleting note 42?
steps.why: In REST the path names the thing (note 42) and the HTTP method names the action (DELETE). One URL per resource, many methods on it.

misconceptions.GET /notes/42/delete: GET must be safe. Crawlers, link prefetchers, and caches send GETs freely, and they would delete your data.
misconceptions.POST /deleteNote?id=42: That's RPC style: the verb lives in the URL. It works, but REST keeps paths as nouns and lets the method carry the action.
misconceptions.DELETE /notes/delete/42: The method already says delete. Putting it in the path too makes the URL name an action instead of the note.

steps.title: Resources are nouns
steps.body: REST models an API as **resources**: nouns with URLs. A plural **collection** (`/books`) holds **items** (`/books/{id}`); nest only for clear ownership (`/users/{id}/books`). The HTTP **method** carries the verb, so the same path does different things.

steps.prompt: Design the API for a simple notes app. Pick a method and a path for each action.

endpoints.purpose: Edit a note's title or text

steps.why: Two URLs cover all five actions: the collection `/notes` and the item `/notes/{id}`. The method picks the action; PATCH changes some fields, while PUT replaces the whole note.

steps.title: Safe and idempotent
steps.body: A method is **safe** if it doesn't change server state (GET). It's **idempotent** if sending it once or ten times leaves the same state (PUT, DELETE). The response may differ (a second DELETE can return 404), but the state doesn't. POST isn't idempotent: each call can create something new.

steps.prompt: Would sending each request twice leave the same server state as sending it once?

items.why: Reads don't change state at all.
Replacing with the same content twice leaves the same note.
The second call finds nothing to delete (maybe a 404), but the state is the same.
PATCH isn't guaranteed idempotent, but this one sets an absolute value, so repeating it changes nothing.
Each call creates another note.
Two calls place two orders.
Relative updates compound: two calls add 2.

steps.why: Idempotency is about the effect on server state, not the method name. Absolute writes (set, replace, delete) are idempotent; creates and relative updates (add, increment) are not.

steps.title: Status codes
steps.body: The status code tells the client what happened before it reads the body. **2xx**: it worked. **4xx**: the client must change something, so retrying as-is won't help (429 is the exception: wait, then retry). **5xx**: the server failed, and a retry may succeed.

rows: Not authenticated: no or bad credentials

steps.prompt: Match each situation to the status code the API should return.
pairs: POST /notes succeeded; the response holds the new note
The request has no auth token at all
A signed-in user tries to delete someone else's note
Sign-up with a username that's already taken
A client sent 500 requests in the last minute; the limit is 100
steps.why: 401 means "who are you?" and 403 means "I know who you are, and no". 409 reports a clash with existing state (some APIs use 400 or 422 for taken usernames), and 429 tells the client to back off.

steps.context: The database is down for ten minutes of planned maintenance, so the API can't serve requests.
steps.prompt: Which status code should the API return?
steps.why: 503 marks a temporary server-side condition and can carry a `Retry-After` header, so clients and load balancers know to back off and try again rather than give up.

misconceptions.500 Internal Server Error: 500 means an unexpected failure, like a bug. 503 says "temporarily unavailable, try later", which is exactly this case.
misconceptions.404 Not Found: The resource exists; the server just can't serve it right now. A 404 could make clients delete their local copy.
misconceptions.400 Bad Request: Nothing is wrong with the request. The problem is on the server side, so it's a 5xx.

lessons.title: Pagination, filtering, and versioning
lessons.summary: Cursors for big feeds, query params for filters, and changing an API without breaking clients.

steps.context: A feed shows newest posts first: page 1 is `?offset=0&limit=20`, page 2 is `?offset=20&limit=20`.
steps.prompt: While a user reads page 1, 5 new posts are published. What do they see on page 2?
options: 5 posts they already saw on page 1
An error, because the offset is stale
steps.answer: 5 posts they already saw on page 1
steps.why: Five new posts push every older post down five slots, so offset 20 now starts at what used to be position 15, and five posts repeat.

misconceptions.A gap: 5 posts are skipped: Gaps happen when rows above the offset are deleted. New rows at the top push everything down, so the windows overlap instead.
misconceptions.Exactly the next 20 posts: An offset counts rows at query time, so it shifts whenever rows are inserted ahead of it.
misconceptions.An error, because the offset is stale: The server has no idea the offset is stale; it happily returns rows 20–39 of the current data.

steps.title: Offset vs cursor pagination
steps.body: **Offset** pagination says "skip N rows"; **cursor** (keyset) pagination says "continue after this item". The cursor is an opaque token holding the last item's sort key, so the query seeks straight to it through an index. Cursors stay correct as rows are inserted and cost the same on page 1 or page 10,000.

left.title: Offset / limit
points: Database reads and discards 4,000 rows first
Duplicates or gaps when rows change

right.title: Cursor (keyset)
points: `WHERE id < :last ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20`

steps.text: In a newest-first feed with increasing ids, the next page asks for posts with an id [[less than]] the last id the client saw. An [[index]] on that column lets the database seek straight to the spot. With `offset=4000`, the database must [[read and discard]] 4,000 rows first.
steps.why: Newest-first means each page holds older, smaller ids, so the cursor condition is `id < last_id`. The index makes that a seek, while an offset forces the database to walk past every skipped row.

steps.context: (A) An internal admin table of 5,000 customers where staff click "page 7". (B) An infinite-scroll feed over billions of posts with constant inserts.
steps.prompt: Which pagination fits each?
options: A: cursor · B: cursor (offset is never acceptable)
steps.why: Offset buys random access at the cost of scale, which is fine on a small, slow-changing table. Cursors give up random access for stability and constant cost, which a large, busy feed needs.

misconceptions.A: cursor · B: cursor (offset is never a: Offset is fine for small, slow-changing data where people want page numbers; skipping a few thousand rows is cheap.
misconceptions.A: offset · B: offset (simplest everywhe: Deep offsets get slower page by page and repeat posts as new ones arrive, exactly what a feed can't afford.
misconceptions.A: cursor · B: offset: Backwards: cursors can't jump to page 7, and offsets break on a busy feed.

steps.title: Filter, sort, and page with query params
steps.body: The **path** names the resource; the **query string** narrows, orders, and pages it. Keep parameter names consistent across endpoints, allow sorting only on indexed fields, and cap `limit` (say, at 100) so one call can't scan the whole table. Return the next cursor in the response.

rows: Page size, capped by the server

steps.prompt: Design endpoints for a blog. Filters, sorting, and cursors go in the query string, so give only the method and path.

endpoints.purpose: List one author's posts, newest first
List the comments on a post
Add a comment to a post

steps.why: Filtering (`?author=42&tag=go`) and paging (`?cursor=…&limit=20`) are query parameters on a collection, not new paths. Nest a collection under its parent (`/posts/{id}/comments`) when the child only makes sense inside it.

steps.title: Changing an API without breaking clients
steps.body: A public API is a promise. **Additive** changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) keep old clients working. **Breaking** changes (renaming, removing, retyping, new required inputs) need a new version, with the old one kept alive through a deprecation window. Put the version in the path or in a header.

left.title: Version in the path
points: Visible in logs, easy to route
Easy to try with curl or a browser
The most common choice for public APIs

right.title: Version in a header
points: URLs name the resource, not the version
Harder to spot in logs and test by hand
Used by Stripe and GitHub (dated versions)

steps.prompt: Would each change break existing clients?

items.text: Add an optional field to a response
items.why: Safe as long as clients ignore fields they don't recognize (a tolerant reader).
Old clients simply don't send it and get the default.
Nothing old calls it, so nothing old changes.
Old clients look for the old name and find nothing.

items.text: Make an optional request field required
items.why: Old clients that omit it start getting 400s.

items.text: Change `price` from a number to a string
items.why: Old clients parse the wrong type.
Old clients that call it get 404s.

steps.why: Old clients must keep working unchanged. Adding things they can ignore is safe; changing or removing anything they already rely on breaks them.

steps.context: Mobile apps in the wild read `user_name`; you want it to be `username`. Many users never update their app.
steps.prompt: What's the best way to make the change?
options: Rename it in place; clients will adapt
Add `username` alongside `user_name`, deprecate the old field, and remove it only in /v2 once old apps fade out
Return 410 Gone to old app versions so users must update
Move the whole API to GraphQL so clients pick their own field names
steps.answer: Add `username` alongside `user_name`, deprecate the old field, and remove it only in /v2 once old apps fade out
steps.why: Additive first, removal later: ship both fields, watch usage of the old one drop, and remove it only in a new version after a deprecation window.

misconceptions.Rename it in place; clients will adapt: Installed app versions break the moment you deploy, and you can't force mobile users to update.
misconceptions.Return 410 Gone to old app versions so u: That cuts off users who did nothing wrong. Forced upgrades are a last resort at the end of a long deprecation window.
misconceptions.Move the whole API to GraphQL so clients: Switching protocols is a far bigger breaking change than the rename it's meant to avoid.

lessons.title: Idempotency, retries, and limits
lessons.summary: Make POSTs safe to retry, back off politely, and authenticate and validate every call.

steps.prompt: A client sends `POST /payments` to charge $50. The request times out before any response arrives. What does the client know?
options: The charge failed, so it's safe to send again
Nothing: the charge may or may not have happened
The server will roll the charge back automatically
steps.answer: Nothing: the charge may or may not have happened
steps.why: A timeout means "no answer", not "no effect". The request may have charged the card and only the response was lost, and resolving that ambiguity is what idempotency keys are for.

misconceptions.The charge failed, so it's safe to send: The request may have reached the server and charged the card. Blindly resending a plain POST can charge twice.
misconceptions.The charge succeeded: The request may never have arrived. Without a response you can't tell.
misconceptions.The server will roll the charge back aut: The server doesn't know the client gave up waiting; a completed charge stays completed.

steps.title: Idempotency keys
steps.body: To make a POST safe to retry, the client creates a unique **idempotency key** (such as a UUID) once per operation and sends it with every attempt: `Idempotency-Key: 4f9c…`. The server stores each key with its result; a repeat returns the saved result instead of charging again. Stripe's API works this way.

steps.prompt: Put a safe payment retry in order.
items: Client generates a unique idempotency key for this payment
Client sends POST /payments with the key in a header
The request times out with no response
Client waits, using exponential backoff with jitter
Client retries the same request with the same key
Server finds the key and returns the original result
steps.why: The key is created before the first attempt and reused unchanged on every retry. That's what lets the server recognize the retry as the same payment rather than a new one.

steps.prompt: In 2–3 sentences: why does an idempotency key stop a retried payment from charging the customer twice?

concepts.label: A timeout leaves the outcome unknown
Every retry carries the same key
The server stores each key with its result
A repeat returns the saved result instead of charging again

steps.model: A timeout means the client doesn't know whether the first charge went through, so it retries with the same idempotency key. The server stores each key with the result of the first attempt, and when a request arrives with a key it has already seen, it returns the stored result instead of charging the card again. However many retries happen, the customer is charged only once.
steps.why: The key turns "did my payment happen?" into a lookup: the first attempt does the work and records its outcome, and every retry just reads that record. The lookup and the charge must be atomic (for example, a unique constraint on the key) so two concurrent retries can't both slip through.

steps.title: Retries, backoff, and 429
steps.body: Retry only what's safe: idempotent methods, or POSTs carrying an idempotency key. Retry on timeouts, 5xx, and **429 Too Many Requests**, not on other 4xx like 400 or 403. Back off exponentially with random **jitter** so thousands of clients don't retry in lockstep, and honor `Retry-After` when the server sends it.

steps.prompt: Should the client retry automatically?

items.why: GET is safe; repeating it can't hurt.
A temporary server-side condition; it may clear in seconds.
Wait the 30 seconds the server asked for, then retry.
PUT is idempotent, and 502 is a server-side failure.

items.text: POST /payments timed out, no idempotency key
items.why: Without a key the server can't tell a retry from a new payment. Check the payment's status first.
The same request will fail the same way; fix it first.
Permissions won't change because you asked again.

steps.why: Retry when the failure is temporary and repeating is harmless. A 4xx other than 429 means the request itself must change, and a POST needs an idempotency key before it's safe to repeat.

steps.title: Tokens and validation
steps.body: Clients log in once, then send a token on each request: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A **JWT** is a signed token holding claims (user id, expiry) that any server can verify with a key, without a session lookup. It's signed, not encrypted: use HTTPS and short expiries. Validate every input and reject bad ones with 400.

steps.prompt: Design a payments API. The create call carries an `Idempotency-Key` header, so its path stays a plain collection.

endpoints.purpose: Check a payment's status after a timeout

steps.why: Payments and refunds are resources you create with POST, so both take idempotency keys. A status GET is the safe way to resolve a timeout before deciding whether to retry.

steps.prompt: A JWT's payload is base64url-encoded and signed. What does the signature guarantee?
options: The claims haven't been altered since the issuer signed them
The claims are encrypted, so no one else can read them
The token can't be stolen and reused
The user is still logged in on the server
steps.answer: The claims haven't been altered since the issuer signed them
steps.why: A signature proves integrity and origin: change one character of the payload and verification fails. It says nothing about secrecy, theft, or current session state.

misconceptions.The claims are encrypted, so no one else: Base64url is an encoding, not encryption; anyone holding the token can decode the payload. Never put secrets in it.
misconceptions.The token can't be stolen and reused: A bearer token works for whoever holds it. That's why it travels only over HTTPS and expires quickly.
misconceptions.The user is still logged in on the serve: Servers verify a JWT without a session lookup, which is also why revoking one before it expires is hard.

lessons.title: Choosing a protocol
lessons.summary: REST, gRPC, or GraphQL, and polling, SSE, or WebSockets for real-time updates.

steps.prompt: A chat app must deliver messages both ways within ~100 ms. Which transport fits best?
steps.why: Chat is two-way, frequent, and latency-sensitive. One persistent, full-duplex WebSocket connection lets either side send a message the instant it exists.

misconceptions.Short polling every 5 seconds: Up to 5 seconds of delay, and most polls come back empty.
misconceptions.Long polling: It works, but each delivered message ends the request and the client must open a new one, adding a round trip and headers per message.
misconceptions.Server-Sent Events: SSE pushes server → client only; sending still needs separate HTTP requests. Workable, but WebSockets give one two-way channel.

steps.title: REST, gRPC, GraphQL
steps.body: **REST**: resources over HTTP and JSON; universal and cacheable, the default for public APIs. **gRPC**: typed calls with Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2; compact, fast, and streaming, ideal between internal services. **GraphQL**: one endpoint where clients ask for exactly the fields they need, handy when many clients want different shapes of the same data.

rows: Varied clients, nested data, one round trip

steps.context: A mobile home screen calls 4 REST endpoints and uses about 10% of each response's fields. On slow mobile networks every round trip hurts.
steps.prompt: Which approach targets exactly this problem?
steps.why: GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs across related objects in a single request, fixing both over-fetching and extra round trips. (On the REST side, a backend-for-frontend endpoint is the usual alternative.)

misconceptions.gRPC: gRPC shrinks payloads and speeds up each call, but every RPC still returns a fixed message, so you'd still make 4 calls or design a new one.
misconceptions.WebSockets: A push channel doesn't fix over-fetching. The problem is the shape of the request, not who starts it.
misconceptions.Short polling: Polling repeats requests; it makes this problem worse, not better.

steps.title: Getting fresh data to clients
steps.body: Four ways to deliver updates, from simplest to most capable. Polling is ordinary HTTP: the client keeps asking. SSE and WebSockets hold one connection open so the server can push the moment something changes; WebSockets also let the client send on the same connection.

rows: Server holds the request until data arrives

steps.prompt: Is polling good enough, or does this need a persistent connection (SSE or WebSockets)?

items.text: Order status that changes a few times an hour
items.why: Checking every 30–60 s is cheap and fresh enough.

items.text: "Your export is ready" after a 10-minute job
items.why: A few seconds of delay on a 10-minute job doesn't matter.

items.text: Daily weather forecast on a dashboard
items.why: It changes a handful of times a day.

items.text: Multiplayer game sending 20 updates per second
items.why: A new HTTP request per update would add latency and overhead to every frame.
They're only useful if they arrive within a fraction of a second.

items.text: Stock prices ticking several times a second
items.why: Updates are constant; polling would either lag or flood the servers.

steps.why: Polling cost grows with how often you ask and how fresh the data must be. Rare updates tolerate a short delay, so plain polling is simpler; frequent or latency-sensitive updates justify holding a connection open.

steps.prompt: Match each use case to the protocol that fits it best.
pairs: Web and mobile clients needing different fields of the same data
Live sports scores pushed to browsers (one-way)
Collaborative whiteboard where everyone draws at once
steps.why: Pick by who the clients are and which way data flows: REST for broad compatibility, gRPC for fast typed internal calls, GraphQL for flexible reads, SSE for one-way push, and WebSockets for two-way real time.

steps.title: Pushing to millions
steps.body: A WebSocket server is **stateful**: it holds open connections for its own slice of users, so no single machine can reach everyone. When something changes, the producing service publishes once to a **pub/sub** channel (Kafka, Redis); every WebSocket server subscribes and pushes the event to the clients it holds.

steps: Each pushes to its connected clients

steps.prompt: Live sports app: when the score service records a goal, push it to 1M connected fans within a second. Wire it up.

nodes.why: Pushing to apps needs servers that hold long-lived connections.
1M connections won't fit on one server; a load balancer spreads them across a pool.

nodes.label: Includes a pub/sub channel (queue or Redis)
nodes.why: Each WebSocket server holds only some fans, so one update must reach all of them.

nodes.label: Includes a score service
nodes.why: Something has to record score changes and publish them.

edges.why: WebSocket servers subscribe to the channel to receive every update.

paths.why: Fans connect through the load balancer to a WebSocket server.
An update flows from the score service through pub/sub to the WebSocket servers and out to fans.

forbidden.why: Clients never talk to the database directly.

steps.why: Fans connect through a load balancer to a pool of WebSocket servers. The score service saves each change and publishes it once, and pub/sub fans it out to every WebSocket server, each pushing to the fans it holds.

steps.context: A news site wants to push breaking headlines to readers' browsers. Readers never send anything back on this channel.
steps.prompt: What's the simplest good fit?
options: gRPC bidirectional streaming from the browser
steps.why: One-way server → browser updates are what SSE is for: a long-lived HTTP response streaming events, with automatic reconnection built into the browser's `EventSource`.

misconceptions.WebSockets: It works, but you'd run a two-way protocol for one-way traffic. SSE is plain HTTP and reconnects (resuming from `Last-Event-ID`) for free.
misconceptions.Short polling every second: Millions of readers each sending a request per second is enormous load for headlines that change a few times an hour.
misconceptions.gRPC bidirectional streaming from the br: Browsers can't speak native gRPC. gRPC-Web, through a proxy, supports only unary and server-streaming calls.
